A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VITA research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original results on eight simulation and two real-world tasks, inference benchmarks, and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v3 reports original results on nine simulation and five real-world tasks, efficiency benchmarks, ablations, and perturbation and unseen-object evaluations.

M1.justification: v3 adds a transformer-based VITA variant using 9×512 spatial features (Section 5.1 and Appendix B.6.2). The original vector-based MLP implementation, action autoencoder, FLD/FLC objectives, and flow procedure remain, making this a bounded architectural extension.

E1.justification: v3 retains the earlier tasks and adds RLBench CloseBox plus three real-world single-arm tasks: PickBall, ToothBrush, and StoreDrawer. Appendix E additionally evaluates manual disturbances during PickBall and four unseen objects during StoreDrawer, substantially expanding task and test-environment coverage.

E2.justification: FM, DP, and ACT remain the principal comparators. v3 adds MLP-based FM with AdaLN to the existing efficiency comparison and evaluates it against MLP-based VITA (Table 1 and Figure 11). Transformer and U-Net FM comparators already appeared in v2; their appearance here is not a new baseline addition.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes VITA's stated training budget from 50K to 25K–50K steps, DP's from 200K to 100K, and ACT's from 200K to 100K–200K. New analyses introduce architecture controls, reward/action-MSE measurements, memory and training-cost benchmarks, and a four-object OOD evaluation. These are substantial reported protocol changes, although v3's DP hyperparameter table still lists 200K steps, leaving that budget inconsistent.

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative evidence for the previously asserted frozen-autoencoder failure, MLP-FM and transformer-VITA architecture comparisons, and FLD training-cost analysis. It also adds DP failure cases, reward and action-MSE analyses, online perturbation examples, and unseen-object tests. Earlier zero-padding, contrastive-loss, variational-encoder, and hyperparameter ablations are largely retained and relocated.

E5.justification: v2 already reports three-seed averages and standard-deviation bands in appendix learning curves. v3 additionally reports mean ± standard deviation for each simulation-table entry (Table 2). The stated seed count remains three; no increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Many existing simulation results change: DP's ThreadNeedle success rate changes from 0% to 59.33%, and VITA's Square result from 100% to 95.33%. v3 also adds CloseBox, single-arm real-world, OOD, architecture, and resource results. VITA's 0.2215 ms MLP latency and the two original real-world task results remain unchanged. Revised training budgets prevent treating the changed simulation scores as established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The FLD/FLC assumption, theorem, lemma, corollaries, and Appendix A proofs are retained. The added Euler update in Section 3 explicates the existing solver, and the repaired assumption cross-reference is editorial rather than a mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The central noise-free vision-to-action flow and action-autoencoder/FLD contributions remain. v3 broadens the architecture claim to include spatial features and transformers, adds quantified memory savings of 18.6%–28.7%, and revises the advertised inference advantage from 1.5×–2.3× to 1.5×–2×. Efficiency receives stronger emphasis without replacing the core contribution.

C2.justification: Appendices B.5–B.8 substantially expand interpretation. v3 attributes DP/ACT failures to precision errors and stringent multi-stage success criteria, connects stochastic visual encodings with lost precision, and explains conditional MLP-FM's difficulties. It also explicitly discusses FLD's additional training time and memory as a tradeoff for inference efficiency, beyond v2's shorter observations.

D1.justification: v3 documents frozen-autoencoder pretraining, the MLP-FM construction, spatial-feature dimensions, and peak-memory measurement using torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated with the shared visual encoder excluded. It adds demonstration counts, camera configurations, and randomization details for the new tasks. It also corrects the DP table to specify the already-described ten-step sampler and explicitly advertises code, datasets, and demos through the retained project-page link.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including π0.5 and Helix for latency motivation, RLBench, and Diffusion as Self-Distillation, with a targeted discussion connecting the latter to latent collapse. The Attention Is All You Need and contrastive predictive coding references are removed. The overall positioning relative to diffusion and cross-modal flow matching remains largely intact.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the efficiency motivation and architecture explanation, condenses the preliminaries, and reorganizes Section 5.2 into efficiency-first and success-rate subsections. The appendices consolidate formerly separate objective discussions and learning-curve sections into an expanded Appendix B, while relocating task and implementation material. This constitutes substantial narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: The efficiency table is redesigned into vector/grid groups with memory reporting, and the simulation table gains uncertainty entries. Figure 4 is rebuilt around five real-world tasks, while the earlier detailed two-task rollout panel moves to Figure 18. New architecture, failure, perturbation, and OOD displays substantially expand the visual evidence; many earlier ablation figures are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency claim through comparable-architecture FM controls, vector/grid comparisons, and explicit memory and training-cost measurements beyond v2's parameter/latency table. Comparative real-world experiments, quantitative frozen-autoencoder evidence, and main-table uncertainty reporting also address important validation gaps. The inconsistent DP training budget and small OOD evaluation limit some conclusions, but the stronger controls and more transparent tradeoff analysis establish a substantial overall improvement.
